title: Vectorization & SIMD
blurb: Tests what SIMD does and where NumPy's speed comes from, why the NumPy speedup collapses past the L3 cache, separating SIMD gains from multi-core gains in BLAS, why data-dependent control flow can't be vectorised, and the common mistakes in each.

refLinks.label: §52.2.1 The Basic Speedup, and Why It Isn’t Constant
§52.2.2 The Cache Cliff: Vectorization’s Speed Ceiling Is Memory Bandwidth
§52.2.3 Separating SIMD From Multi-Core: The Matmul Breakdown
§52.2.4 The Honest Counter-Example: Data-Dependent Control Flow Defeats Vectorization

questions.prompt: How many float64 values fit in one 256-bit AVX2 register?
questions.explanation: A float64 is 64 bits, and 256 / 64 = 4. One instruction then works on four values at once.

questions.prompt: Where does NumPy's speed over a Python loop come from, per the chapter?
options: Running each element on a separate GPU thread
NumPy being a faster Python interpreter for every kind of code
Compiled, vectorised loops and BLAS libraries that use SIMD directly
Caching the results of earlier calls
questions.explanation: NumPy isn't "faster Python" in general. Its array operations run as compiled loops, often via OpenBLAS, that use SIMD. Python-level loops over arrays get none of that.

questions.prompt: At n = 1,000,000, the Python loop took 34.859 ms and NumPy 0.2357 ms. What is the speedup? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 34.859 / 0.2357 = 147.9, the peak of the four sizes tested, before it fell to 11.2x at 10 million.

refLinks.label: §52.2.1 The Basic Speedup, and Why It Isn’t Constant

questions.prompt: Between which working-set sizes did NumPy's throughput fall off a cliff?
options: Between 1 MB and 2 MB, the size of L1
Above 160 MB only, past main memory
Between 16 MB and 32 MB, the size of L2
Between 64 MB and 96 MB, around the 64 MB L3
questions.explanation: 64.4 GB/s at 16 MB fell to 4.4 GB/s at 96 MB and stayed flat. The chapter ties it to the 64 MB L3.

refLinks.label: §52.2.2 The Cache Cliff: Vectorization’s Speed Ceiling Is Memory Bandwidth

questions.prompt: Past the cliff, why doesn't better vectorisation help?
options: The CPU lowers its clock speed for large arrays.
NumPy turns off SIMD for arrays bigger than the L3 cache.
Large arrays are processed one element at a time by the interpreter.
It's memory-bound now. SIMD speeds compute.
questions.explanation: Once data comes from beyond the cache, compute was never the limit. The fix is less data movement: better layout, smaller dtypes or chunking.

refLinks.label: §52.2.2 The Cache Cliff: Vectorization’s Speed Ceiling Is Memory Bandwidth

questions.prompt: Using Listing 52.2's formula, what is the implied bandwidth for 10,000,000 float64 elements, 2 arrays touched, in 0.0387 s? Give one decimal place in GB/s.
How did the chapter isolate the SIMD-only part of NumPy's matmul speed?
options: It ran the matmul in a pure Python loop for comparison.
It disabled SIMD and compared against the default build.
It set OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, so only one core was used.
It used smaller matrices that fit in a single cache line.
questions.explanation: One thread removes the multi-core part, leaving SIMD and cache blocking on one core, about 68 GFLOPS at every size.

refLinks.label: §52.2.3 Separating SIMD From Multi-Core: The Matmul Breakdown

questions.prompt: A matmul of two n × n matrices does about 2n³ floating-point operations. How many GFLOPs is that for n = 1,000?
questions.explanation: 2 × 1000³ = 2 × 10^9 operations, which is 2 GFLOP. At about 68 GFLOPS single-threaded, that takes roughly 29 ms.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 52.3 run each version in a separate subprocess?
options: Two matmuls can't run in the same Python process.
Subprocesses avoid the GIL, which would slow the matmul.
OpenBLAS reads the thread setting once, at start-up.
The timing is only accurate in a fresh process.
questions.explanation: Setting OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS after NumPy has loaded usually has no effect. The procedure's common mistake is toggling it inside one session.

questions.prompt: Why check np.show_config() on a new deployment?
options: A bare BLAS build can be far slower, silently.
It shows how many arrays are currently in memory.
It is required before NumPy can use more than one core.
It switches NumPy to its fastest backend automatically.
questions.explanation: An unusual platform or a bare container can fall back to reference BLAS silently. show_config shows whether OpenBLAS or MKL is linked.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't the Collatz workload be vectorised?
options: Each element loops a data-dependent number of times.
The list of 20,000 numbers was too short for NumPy.
The numbers are integers, and SIMD only works on floats.
Collatz needs recursion, which NumPy doesn't support.
questions.explanation: SIMD applies one shared operation to many values. Here every element loops an unpredictable number of times. SIMD handles integers fine, and the code isn't recursive.

refLinks.label: §52.2.4 The Honest Counter-Example: Data-Dependent Control Flow Defeats Vectorization

questions.prompt: The "NumPy" Collatz version ran at 0.98x. Why no gain?
options: The array was copied twice, which cost more than the loop saved.
NumPy runs integer arithmetic more slowly than Python does.
It still calls Python once per element.
NumPy can't store integers larger than 2³¹.
questions.explanation: Wrapping a Python loop in an array call doesn't vectorise it. np.vectorize has the same problem.

refLinks.label: §52.2.4 The Honest Counter-Example: Data-Dependent Control Flow Defeats Vectorization

options: Converting the result back to a list at the end
Using float64 instead of float32
Converting to an array but still looping over it in Python
Writing the operation as whole-array arithmetic
questions.explanation: [f(x) for x in arr] passes every element through the interpreter. The operation has to be expressed as arithmetic on whole arrays.

questions.prompt: Which of these is truly vectorised?
options: np.where(arr > 0, arr * 2.0, 0.0)
[x * 2.0 if x > 0 else 0.0 for x in arr.tolist()]
"\"np.vectorize(lambda x: x * 2.0 if x > 0 else 0.0)(arr)\""
np.array([x * 2.0 if x > 0 else 0.0 for x in arr])
questions.explanation: np.where runs the comparison and both branches as compiled whole-array operations. np.vectorize and list comprehensions call Python per element.

questions.prompt: Where does the chapter say vectorisation won't help? Select all that apply.
options: The same arithmetic applied to every element of a large array
Per-element control flow or iteration counts that depend on the data
Work that is already memory-bandwidth-bound
Graph traversal, parsing and recursive algorithms
questions.explanation: Data-dependent work has no shared operation, and bandwidth-bound work isn't limited by compute. Uniform elementwise arithmetic is exactly what vectorisation is for.

questions.prompt: A vectorised NumPy step on 200 MB arrays shows an implied bandwidth near the chapter's flat region. A teammate wants to hand-tune SIMD intrinsics. What does Procedure 52.2 suggest?
options: Hand-tune the intrinsics, since NumPy's SIMD is generic.
Check if it's memory-bound, then cut data movement.
Add more threads, since bandwidth scales with core count.
Switch to Python loops, which use less memory per element.
questions.explanation: The procedure's common mistake is seeking better vectorisation for an operation already limited by memory. Layout, smaller dtypes or chunking are the levers there.

bookExercises.prompt: In your own words, explain why the Python-vs-NumPy speedup in Listing 52.5 grows across the first three sizes but collapses at $n=10{,}000{,}000$. Name the specific hardware boundary responsible.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: For $n \le 1{,}000{,}000$, the read-plus-write working set fits inside this CPU's 64MB L3 cache, so throughput is limited mainly by how fast the SIMD units can issue instructions, and that throughput improves as fixed per-call overhead is amortized over more elements. At $n=10{,}000{,}000$ the working set (roughly 160MB counting the input, output, and an intermediate temporary) exceeds the 64MB L3 cache, so the operation becomes a genuine round-trip to DRAM on every access. The specific hardware boundary responsible is the 64MB L3 cache on the reference rig's Ryzen 9 5950X.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague says "vectorization always makes code faster." Using the Collatz result from Listing 52.7, write two or three sentences correcting this claim precisely.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Vectorization only makes code faster when the same operation applies uniformly to every element with no data-dependent branching or per-element iteration count. The Collatz example violates this directly, each number requires a different, data-determined number of steps, so wrapping the loop in NumPy array syntax produced a 0.98x "speedup," i.e. no benefit at all, because there was no shared structure for a SIMD instruction to exploit in the first place.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 52.2's `implied_bandwidth_gb_s` function, compute the implied bandwidth for an operation touching two `float32` arrays of 5,000,000 elements each (read one, write the other) that takes 8.5 ms. State whether this looks compute-bound or memory-bound given this chapter's ~4-64 GB/s range.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Total bytes moved = 5,000,000 elements × 4 bytes (`float32`) × 2 arrays touched = 40,000,000 bytes = 0.04 GB. Implied bandwidth = 0.04 GB / 0.0085 s ≈ 4.7 GB/s. That figure sits right at the flattened tail of this chapter's cache-cliff table (4.1-4.4 GB/s once the working set exceeds L3), so this operation looks memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. Further vectorization effort would not move this number.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 52.4, run `np.show_config()` in your own environment and report which BLAS backend is in use. If it isn't OpenBLAS or MKL, propose one concrete next step before trusting any NumPy performance numbers from that environment.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion/lab exercise, no single answer, since the result depends on the reader's own environment. If `np.show_config()` reports `openblas` or `mkl` with a CPU-specific dispatch note (e.g. `DYNAMIC_ARCH`, `SkylakeX`), the backend is properly vectorized. If it reports a generic/reference BLAS or no BLAS section at all, the concrete next step is to reinstall NumPy from a build that links a real BLAS (e.g. `pip install numpy` from a wheel with OpenBLAS bundled, or a conda environment using `conda-forge`'s NumPy, which links OpenBLAS by default) before trusting any timing numbers from that environment.

bookExercises.prompt: The matmul breakdown shows single-threaded NumPy holding ~68 GFLOPS across three matrix sizes while multi-threaded performance varies from 257 to 495 GFLOPS. Propose a reason the multi-threaded number doesn't scale as cleanly with size as the single-threaded number does.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Multi-threaded matmul performance depends on how well the problem size divides across 16 cores and fits each core's per-thread working set into its own cache, plus thread-scheduling and synchronization overhead that doesn't apply to the single-threaded case at all. At 500×500 the matrices are small enough that thread-launch overhead eats into the gain: 378.1 GFLOPS is a solid ~5.4x over single-threaded, but not the ~16x a naive "one core per size" model would predict. At 2000×2000 the problem is large enough to amortize that overhead well, pushing 495.5 GFLOPS, but 1000×1000 sits in an awkward middle where cache-blocking boundaries interact less favorably with 16-way partitioning, producing the lowest multi-threaded figure (257.4 GFLOPS) of the three. The single-threaded number stays flat because it isn't subject to any of these partitioning effects. It's purely the SIMD throughput of one core's ALUs.

bookExercises.prompt: A teammate proposes wrapping a recursive tree-traversal function in `np.vectorize` to "vectorize" it. Using Procedure 52.1's common mistake and this chapter's Collatz example, explain why this will not produce a SIMD speedup, and propose what question to ask about the workload before attempting any vectorization.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `np.vectorize` (and a list comprehension over a NumPy array) still calls back into the Python interpreter once per element. It does not generate a single SIMD instruction covering multiple elements, so it gets none of the speedup this chapter measured for whole-array arithmetic. A recursive tree traversal is structurally identical to the Collatz counter-example: each node visited requires a data-dependent number of recursive calls and branches, so there is no shared, uniform operation for a SIMD instruction to apply across "elements" in the first place. The question to ask before attempting any vectorization: does every element go through the exact same sequence of operations regardless of its own value? If the answer is no, as it is for both Collatz and tree traversal, vectorization has nothing to exploit, and the right next move is a different kind of optimization entirely (a compiled/JIT'd loop, or restructuring the traversal to be iterative and batchable, not a NumPy wrapper).

bookExercises.prompt: A production service processes a working set of about 200MB per request on hardware similar to this chapter's reference rig. Using the cache-cliff table, predict roughly what implied bandwidth this request should see, and state one architectural change (not a NumPy trick) that could improve it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A 200MB working set falls well past this chapter's cache-cliff table, which flattens to roughly 4.1-4.4 GB/s once the working set exceeds ~96MB, so a 200MB request should land in that same flattened 4-5 GB/s range, not the 24-64 GB/s seen when the working set still fits in L3. One architectural change that would actually move this number: process the request in smaller chunks that each fit within the 64MB L3 boundary (streaming/chunking, Chapter 54), so more of the working set is served from cache rather than DRAM on each pass, a data-movement fix, not a compute-side one, since the bottleneck here is bandwidth, not arithmetic throughput.

bookExercises.prompt: Read enough of Intel's Intrinsics Guide to find the AVX2 instruction for a 256-bit packed double-precision multiply. Explain, at a level a colleague without an assembly background could follow, how that single instruction relates to the "4 `float64`s in one register" claim this chapter opens with.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, the relevant instruction is `_mm256_mul_pd`, which multiplies two `__m256d` registers, each holding four packed double-precision (`float64`) values, in a single instruction. The "4 `float64`s in one register" claim maps directly onto this: a 256-bit AVX2 register holds exactly 4 × 64 bits, and `_mm256_mul_pd` performs four independent multiplications, one per lane, in the time a single scalar multiply instruction would take for one value. This is the literal hardware mechanism underneath every "vectorized" NumPy operation in this chapter. NumPy/OpenBLAS's compiled loops emit instructions like this one (or their AVX-512 equivalents) instead of a scalar multiply repeated in a loop.
